bodyMarkdown:
## The idea in plain language

A stacked bar is several bar charts balanced on top of each other. The whole column tells you the total; each coloured band tells you one component's contribution.

The catch is that only the bottom band starts at zero. Every band above it has to be read as a **difference** between two boundary lines, which is where careless reading costs marks.

## What is actually going on

Two questions get asked. Absolute questions ask for one band's size — read the gap between its top and bottom edges. Proportional questions ask for a component's share of its column — divide the band by the column total.

Watch for the difference between a component **growing** and its **share** growing. A component can increase in absolute terms while its share falls, if the total grew faster.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Quarterly sales stack as Electronics 45, Apparel 30, Groceries 25 in Q1. What share of Q1 came from Electronics?

formulaCards.title: Reading a band
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: A band's value is (its top edge) minus (its bottom edge), not its top edge alone.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A band running from 45 to 75 on the axis represents 30, not 75.

formulaCards.title: Share within a column
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A band of 30 in a column totalling 120 is a 25 percent share.

commonTraps: Reading a band's top edge as its value instead of subtracting the bottom edge.
Confusing growth in absolute size with growth in share.
Comparing bands across columns of different heights without converting to shares.
